title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Message Syntax and Routing
summary: Gives an overview of HTTP architecture and terminology, defines the http and https URI schemes, and specifies the HTTP/1.1 message syntax, parsing requirements, and related security concerns. It was part of the RFC 7230 series that replaced RFC 2616. It was later replaced by RFC 9110 and RFC 9112.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7230 defines the structure of HTTP/1.1 messages and how clients route them to servers or proxies. Its framing rules tell a recipient where headers end and how to determine the end of a message body.

questions: what is the http message syntax
http and https uri scheme definition
how does http determine message body length
subtitle: The structure, routing and connection rules for HTTP/1.1 messages.

tldr.problem: HTTP participants need to parse messages consistently and determine where each message body ends, especially when requests pass through intermediaries.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines message lines and headers, four request-target forms, rules for Host and body length, chunked transfer coding and persistent connections.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7230 obsoleted RFC 2145 and RFC 2616. It has been obsoleted by RFC 9110 and RFC 9112 and updated by RFC 8615.

sections.title: HTTP Roles and URI Schemes
sections.content:
HTTP is a stateless request/response protocol. A client sends a request over a connection, and a server returns a response; the client and server labels describe roles for that connection.

The RFC defines the http and https URI schemes. The default TCP ports are 80 for http and 443 for https. For https, the user agent must establish a strongly encrypted, end-to-end connection before sending the first request.
sections.plainLanguage: An HTTP client sends a request and a server answers it. The URI scheme and authority identify the destination and whether the connection must use TLS.

sections.title: The Shape of a Message
sections.content:
An HTTP/1.1 message has a start-line, zero or more header fields, an empty line and an optional body. A request start-line contains a method, request-target and version; a response start-line contains a version, status code and reason phrase.

Header names are case-insensitive. A recipient must parse the message as octets in an encoding compatible with US-ASCII, rather than first interpreting the whole message as Unicode text.
sections.plainLanguage: The first line says what the request asks or how the response went. Headers follow, then a blank line marks the start of any message body.

sections.title: Message Bodies and Their Length
sections.content:
HTTP recipients use message headers and status rules to determine whether a body exists and how long it is. A valid Content-Length gives the body size in octets. A response without another length rule can end when the server closes the connection.

Chunked transfer coding sends data in chunks, each with a hexadecimal size, and ends with a zero-sized chunk and an empty line. This lets a sender stream a body whose total size is not known in advance. A recipient must be able to decode chunked messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender and recipient need the same rule for finding the end of a body. A length field gives its size, or chunked coding marks the end with a zero-sized chunk.

sections.title: Request Targets and the Host Field
sections.content:
HTTP defines four request-target forms. Origin-form carries a path and optional query for a direct request; absolute-form carries the full URI to a proxy; authority-form is used for CONNECT; asterisk-form is used for a server-wide OPTIONS request.

Every HTTP/1.1 request must contain a Host field. It carries the target authority so a server can distinguish names that share an IP address. A proxy can forward a request and record intermediaries in a Via field.
sections.plainLanguage: The request-target changes with the request method and whether the client is using a proxy. The Host field identifies the requested host so the server can select the right resource.

sections.title: Persistent Connections
sections.content:
HTTP/1.1 connections persist by default, so one connection can carry more than one request and response. A Connection field can indicate that the connection should close after the current response.

Messages on a persistent connection need a body length that does not depend on connection closure. A server must read a whole request body or close the connection after responding, so leftover body bytes are not mistaken for a later request.
sections.plainLanguage: A persistent connection carries several exchanges without reconnecting. Each message still needs a clear end so its remaining bytes are not read as a new request.

sections.title: Parsing and Security Risks
sections.content:
The RFC warns that different parsers can disagree about message boundaries. Request smuggling uses such differences to hide an additional request, while response splitting exploits disagreement about response boundaries.

The body-length rules specify how Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length interact. When both appear, the RFC says Transfer-Encoding takes precedence and recommends treating the message as an error because it may indicate an attack.
sections.plainLanguage: If two HTTP participants disagree about where a message ends, one may see an extra hidden request. Clear and consistent framing rules reduce this risk.
